content:
This is something which has annoyed me endlessly in the past, and I think @ZhiKai Pong has just experienced the same pain. So let me ask here:

In PhysLib when I have a branch A, then make branch B based on A, if I make a pull-request from A and from B independently, the changes from A show in the pull-request made from B. This happens even after A is merged with master.

This makes the task of splitting PRs or basing a branch of a PR which is not master a bit of a nightmare. Does anyone know what settings we would have to change to make this experience nicer?

to be honest I think this is more of a git thing, but any tips and advices could be helpful. What I did was git rebase after the first PR gets merged, then force push to update the branch of the second PR.
I would do what @ZhiKai Pong describes: the second PR is not ready to be reviewed until the first PR was merged, and everything is fine.

I'm guessing what you're saying is you create BranchA and start work on a new feature, then create BranchB by clicking New Branch on the github branch page and then creating BranchB with source BranchA?

Daniel Morrison said:

I'm guessing what you're saying is you create BranchA and start work on a new feature, then create BranchB by clicking New Branch on the github branch page and then creating BranchB with source BranchA?

Basically but you will want to rebase the second one from master once your first PR is in, since there are likely other commits too.

And the merged branch might have code review suggestions implemented etc. since you made your next one.
Sorry, I intended to ask Joseph if that was the steps he was taking.
My bad , thought you were replying to Michael
No it makes sense I wasn't thinking about it that way so I didn't think to clarify!

Daniel Morrison said:

I'm guessing what you're saying is you create BranchA and start work on a new feature, then create BranchB by clicking New Branch on the github branch page and then creating BranchB with source BranchA?

Yep this is what I'm doing :).

To rebase, is git rebase enough, or does one have to force it somehow? I recall getting some message about history been overwritten when I did something like this in the past. I.e. could someone write down the full command one would need to run on BranchB. Thanks.
CC @Yaël Dillies

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

Yep this is what I'm doing :).

My understanding is that when you say the source is BranchA you are not only using that code as your starting point but also git is tracking changes starting from that point in BranchA, so when you try to merge BranchB into main you get weird results because the history doesn't match up. The way I think of it is when I say that BranchAis the source of BranchB I am expecting to merge BranchB back into BranchA - the source is also where you will want to merge to in the future. So if you want to eventually merge into main, you want main to be your source.

Instead I would create a new branch with source master and then move code over to the new branch. It's a tad more work to move code over but it saves from git headaches like this.

What I usually do is make new branches on my local copy with git switch -c <new-branch> which to my understanding creates a duplicate of the current branch with all the history back to the main branch. Then I get a copy of all the code but the base is still master and merging PRs is nicer.

I am by no means a git expert and I could very well be wrong with how this all works but this process has served me well, however it works.

I would also recommend trying to learn to do as much from the command line as possible, as often the UI shortcuts in Github/VSCode will hide some aspects from you which seems safer but it actually can make it harder to fix when something goes wrong.
Someone who knows more can probably give a better answer than I can, but that's my "I want to avoid thinking about git as much as possible" answer.

I like this way of thinking about this - thank you.

This:

Instead I would create a new branch with source master and then move code over to the new branch. It's a tad more work to move code over but it saves from git headaches like this.

does seem like a pain though, unless there is someway to automatically copy all o the changes across with something like checkout.

here's the commands I ran: after making sure everything I want is in BranchB (e.g. after git merge master), do

git rebase -X theirs origin/master
-- (uses `BranchB` for all conflicts by default)

git rebase -i origin/master
-- (interactive window, change all commits to squash)

git push --force origin BranchB

maybe there's a better way to do this but this doesn't seem that bad (figuring this out in the first place is annoying though).

I'd use squash-and-merge / rebase-and-merge. They are needed to have a clean commit history. E.g. this unnecessarily got committed to master: https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib/commit/7fe468fc1d417d206e22b3822116fed3c9454e08 , and the surrounding commits that are named "fixes", "fixes", etc.
In the GitHub admin page, you can disable the merge-only button so that it doesn't happen.
With squash-and-merge (the button on GitHub), you don't have to bother with the duplicated commits at all.

Rein Zustand said:

With squash-and-merge (the button on GitHub), you don't have to bother with the duplicated commits at all.

The issue was if I just do git merge PR1, the diff shows all of PR1's changes as well, making it difficult to review. My understanding is that it is necessary to rebase to master branch to clean up the diff?

@Rein Zustand I don't think this addresses the diff issue, but thank you for mentioning that you can tun off the merge-only button. I have just done this for PhysLib, since I do not see any setting where we should be using this.

ZhiKai Pong said:

Rein Zustand said:

With squash-and-merge (the button on GitHub), you don't have to bother with the duplicated commits at all.

The issue was if I just do git merge PR1, the diff shows all of PR1's changes as well, making it difficult to review. My understanding is that it is necessary to rebase to master branch to clean up the diff?

I think you don't need to constantly rebase, with squash-and-merge. AFAIU, squash and merge compares the final version of the PR branch and the master branch, and then calculate the resulting diff. Also, I was referring to GitHub's squash-and-merge button instead of git merge PR1.

For comparison, Zulip devs use rebase-and-merge, but this is because they curate every single commit carefully. And yes, for stale branches, they usually ask contributors to rebase their PR's.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

I like this way of thinking about this - thank you.

This:

Instead I would create a new branch with source master and then move code over to the new branch. It's a tad more work to move code over but it saves from git headaches like this.

does seem like a pain though, unless there is someway to automatically copy all o the changes across with something like checkout.

I don't know of a way to do this within GitHub, but what I was saying about doing git switch -c <new-branch> from the old branch will do what you want. What I've done in the past is create the new branch on GitHub (source master) so git can connect the remote branch automatically then use git switch on my local version to duplicate the branch and push the results to the GitHub branch.

There are probably easier ways to do this and this is not the "correct" way to do this but it keeps me out of trouble
